subject: chemistry
title: Storage cells and fuel cells
key_idea: A storage cell makes electricity from a redox reaction between chemicals stored inside it, and it can be recharged if the reaction is reversible. A fuel cell is supplied with a fuel and oxygen continuously, so it never needs recharging.

blocks.text: Cells turn chemical energy into electrical energy. This section covers non-rechargeable and rechargeable cells and how to use electrode data on them.

items.meaning: A cell whose reaction is irreversible. It stops when the reactants are used up.
A cell whose reaction can be reversed by passing a current through it in the opposite direction.

items: Each electrode reaction is a half-equation with an Eᶿ value. The more positive electrode is the positive terminal.
The emf of the cell is Eᶿ(positive) − Eᶿ(negative).
Oxidation happens at the negative electrode. Reduction happens at the positive electrode.
On recharging, the electrode reactions run in reverse and the cell is restored.
Positive electrode: Li⁺ + CoO₂ + e⁻ → Li⁺[CoO₂]⁻
Negative electrode: Li → Li⁺ + e⁻
Overall: Li + CoO₂ → Li⁺[CoO₂]⁻
Electrons flow through the external circuit from the lithium electrode to the cobalt oxide electrode. Li⁺ ions move through the electrolyte.
Lithium has a very negative Eᶿ, so lithium cells give a high voltage.

items.text: Write each half-equation with its Eᶿ.
The more negative Eᶿ is the negative electrode and is oxidised.
Add the half-equations, cancel the electrons and subtract Eᶿ values to get the emf.

items: A rechargeable cell has reversible electrode reactions.
The negative electrode is oxidised and the positive electrode is reduced.
The emf is Eᶿ(positive) − Eᶿ(negative).

blocks.text: A fuel cell uses the energy from a fuel reacting with oxygen to make a voltage. This section covers the hydrogen–oxygen cell.

items: The fuel and oxygen are fed in continuously. The cell does not need recharging.
Hydrogen is common. Methanol and other hydrogen-rich fuels are also used.
The only product of a hydrogen–oxygen cell is water.
Electrons flow from the hydrogen electrode (negative) to the oxygen electrode (positive) through the external circuit.

blocks.text: In both cells the overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Each electrode is a porous surface with a catalyst, such as platinum, so the gases can react.

diagram.alt: Sort statements into non-rechargeable cells, rechargeable cells and fuel cells.
diagram.prompt: Sort each statement into the right type of cell.

items.text: The cell stops when the reactants are used up
A current in the reverse direction restores the reactants
It can be used many times, with charging in between
Hydrogen and oxygen are supplied continuously
It is thrown away once the reactants are used up

items: A fuel cell is supplied with fuel and oxygen. It does not need recharging.
In an acidic cell, H⁺ forms at the negative electrode. In an alkaline cell, OH⁻ is used there.
Overall: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

blocks.text: Every cell has benefits and risks. This section covers those for rechargeable and fuel cells.

rows: They can be reused many times. They are light and store a lot of energy.
Lithium and cobalt must be mined. Disposal and fires are risks if the cell is damaged or overheated.
The only product is water. They are efficient and do not need recharging.
Hydrogen is flammable and hard to store. It is often made from fossil fuels, which release CO₂.
They are cheap and need no charger.
They are used once and thrown away. Their metals are lost as waste.

items: Fuel cells make only water, but the hydrogen has to be produced and stored.
Rechargeable cells reduce waste but need mined metals.

checks.q: Write the half-equation at the negative electrode of an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
State one difference between a fuel cell and a rechargeable cell.
checks.a: A fuel cell is supplied continuously with a fuel and oxygen and does not need recharging. A rechargeable cell holds its chemicals inside and must be recharged with an electric current.

checks.q: A cell has electrode reactions with Eᶿ = +0.80 V and Eᶿ = −0.44 V. Identify the negative electrode and calculate the emf.
checks.a: The −0.44 V electrode is negative and is oxidised. Emf = +0.80 − (−0.44) = +1.24 V.

items: Details of storage cells, equations and electrode potential data are provided in the exam. You apply the principles to them.
You do not need to recall fuel cells or their equations. You explain what happens at each electrode from the data given.
Know the electrode reactions of the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with both acidic and alkaline electrolytes.
Know that methanol and other hydrogen-rich fuels are used in fuel cells.
Learn the simplified lithium cell reactions given above. You use electrode data to deduce the reactions in non-rechargeable and rechargeable cells.

Explain how the electrode reactions generate an electric current: oxidation releases electrons at the negative electrode, they flow round the external circuit, and reduction uses them at the positive electrode.
Fuel cells generate a current and do not need electrical recharging.
